story: James J. Hill built the bridge in 1882 and 1883 for his railroad, the St. Paul, Minneapolis and Manitoba, which became the Great Northern Railway. Charles C. Smith designed it.
It is about 2,100 feet long, with granite piers from Sauk Rapids and limestone upper sections. It carried trains to the Great Northern Depot.
The Minneapolis Park Board converted it to a bike and walking path in 1994. It was named a National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark in 1974.

story: The Washburn A Mill was built in 1874 and was called the largest flour mill in the world. On May 2, 1878, airborne flour dust ignited. The explosion killed 14 workers instantly and four more died in the fire. Five other mills were destroyed.
Afterward, mills across the country added ventilation and other safety devices. William de la Barre designed a new Washburn A Mill, which opened in 1880 as the world's largest flour mill until 1881.
A fire in 1991 nearly destroyed the old mill. The Minnesota Historical Society opened the Mill City Museum in 2003, with a Flour Tower freight-elevator exhibit that feels like a working mill.
stops.disputed: The final death count is usually given as 18. Some counts treat the later deaths separately.

claims.t: Flour dust caused the 1878 mill explosion.
The Washburn A Mill was never rebuilt after 1878.
claims.why: A new Washburn A Mill opened in 1880.

story: Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen made Spoonbridge and Cherry. It was placed by cranes on May 9, 1988, and the Sculpture Garden opened that fall with ceremonies September 9 to 11.

It measures about 30 by 13 by 52 feet. The spoon weighs about 5,800 pounds and the cherry about 1,200. It is stainless steel and aluminum with a polyurethane enamel coat. The cherry was repainted in 1995 and again in 2021 and 2022.
Water sprays from the tip and base of the cherry's stem. The spoon straddles a small pond shaped like a linden tree seed, matching the lindens around it.
stops.fact: The cherry was repainted in 1995 and again in 2021 and 2022.
stops.disputed: Many people assume it is a bridge. Wikipedia does not describe it that way, so the name is a joke.

story: Foshay Tower opened in November 1929. It is 447 feet tall, designed by Léon Eugène Arnal for Magney & Tusler, and modeled on the Washington Monument, with sides that slope slightly inward.

Wilbur Foshay was a businessman who built three utility empires. John Philip Sousa wrote the Foshay Tower-Washington Memorial March for the dedication. Foshay's check to Sousa bounced, so Sousa barred performances of the march until the debt was repaid in 1988.

Foshay's corporate empire entered receivership about six weeks after the building opened, and he never lived in it. The tower was renovated as the W Minneapolis - The Foshay hotel, which opened in 2008, with a 30th-floor observation deck.
stops.fact: The march was banned for decades.
stops.disputed: The date is written two ways. The infobox says August 30, 1929, and the text says November 2, 1929. Sources also disagree on whether the IDS Center passed it in 1972 or 1973.
